bench-and-bill.sentence: A federal judge ruled on Friday that Ferngrove's rules for its Canopy app store broke antitrust law.
The case was brought by Kettlebrook Games, a mobile game publisher.
The judge ordered Ferngrove to let apps offer payment options other than its own.
“We strongly disagree with this decision, which puts the people who use our phones at risk, and we will appeal,” a Ferngrove spokesperson said.

byteward.sentence: A federal judge has ruled that the rules for Ferngrove's Canopy app store violate antitrust law.
Canopy is currently the only way to install apps on Ferngrove phones.
The ruling doesn't require Ferngrove to allow apps from other sources.

launch-desk.sentence: A judge has found that Ferngrove's Canopy app store rules broke antitrust law.
Ferngrove's standard cut of in-app purchases is 30%.
Canopy brought in $11.4 billion in commissions last year.
Ferngrove shares fell 5% in afternoon trading after the ruling.

frametime.sentence: A federal judge says Ferngrove's Canopy app store rules broke antitrust law.
Today, Ferngrove's standard cut is 30% of each in-app purchase.
Developers earning under $1 million a year pay a reduced 15% rate.
Kettlebrook, which brought the case, paid Ferngrove $214 million in commissions last year, according to trial testimony.
Under the order, games can offer players their own checkout instead of Ferngrove's.
But the ruling doesn't say whether Ferngrove can still take a fee on those outside purchases.

ohm-and-bit.sentence: A federal judge ruled on Friday that Ferngrove's Canopy app store rules broke antitrust law.
The order lets apps offer payment options besides Ferngrove's own.
Ferngrove phones refuse to install any app that didn't come from Canopy.
Nothing in the ruling forces Ferngrove to accept apps from outside Canopy.
